query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, adherent, alumina-forming diffusion-barrier coating to a refractory high-entropy alloy will significantly reduce high-temperature oxidation by creating a stable Al2O3 surface scale that impedes oxygen ingress under service temperatures of at least 1200 °C in air.
generation.material_initial_state: Baseline refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., MoNbTaTiW-based) in as-cast or homogenized condition without protective coating
generation.intervention: Surface modification by pack aluminizing (or analogous sputter deposition) to deposit an aluminum-rich layer that generates an alumina (Al2O3) scale in oxidizing environments
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure above 1200 °C in air for at least 100 hours
generation.structural_mediator: Formed Al2O3 coating working as a stable, low-permeability oxygen diffusion barrier
generation.mechanism: Upon heating, the aluminized surface reacts with oxygen to form a dense, continuous Al2O3 film that inhibits further oxidation by blocking oxygen diffusion into the alloy substrate
generation.predicted_outcome: A marked reduction in mass gain (≥50% lower weight gain than the uncoated alloy) and improved structural integrity (significantly reduced scale spallation) relative to the untreated alloy under the specified conditions
generation.baseline: Untreated refractory high-entropy alloys often experience rapid oxidation and scale spallation above 1200 °C in air, leading to significant weight gain and surface degradation within 100 hours
generation.boundary: At temperatures beyond 1400 °C or in more aggressive environments (e.g., combustion gases with contaminants), coating stability and adhesion may degrade, limiting the intervention’s effectiveness
generation.uncertainty: Exact long-term adhesion behavior and spallation risk beyond 200 hours is not fully established for all RHEA chemistries

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy coupons (untreated vs. pack-aluminized) of the same base RHEA composition, then heat both sets in air at 1200 °C for up to 200 hours while tracking weight change at regular intervals.
measurements: Mass gain per unit area vs. time for each sample
Microstructural evaluation (SEM/EDS) on oxide scale after exposure
Surface hardness to monitor coating integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the mass gain and oxide morphology of the coated samples do not differ significantly from the untreated condition (showing similar oxidation kinetics and scale spallation), then the hypothesis that an alumina-forming coating decreases high-temperature oxidation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As the temperature capability of modern Ni- based superalloys has reached its limit for gas turbine engine applications, materials scientists are searching for new materials with higher temperature capabilities. Recently, “High-Entropy Alloy (HEA)” [1] , [2] has been proposed as a new strategy for alloy design with a wide composition space. Other names such as “compositionally complex alloys (CCAs)” has also been given to this class of alloy containing multiple phases [3] . Nevertheless, the alloy design strategy of HEA/CCA shows great promise for exploring new alloy systems. RHEA was first proposed by Senkov et al . [4] as an attempt to create new alloy systems for high temperature applications beyond superalloys. By combining refractory elements such as W, Mo, Ta, Nb, Hf, …etc. in equi- or near equi-molar ratios, several RHEAs with promising mechanical properties have been reported [5] – [7] . However, oxidation resistance is crucial since it could lead to severe degradation in mechanical properties. Abstract In this paper, the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating was prepared on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method. The microstructural evolution and compositions of the silicide coating under high-temperature oxidation environment were studied. The results show that the silicide coating could effectively prevent the oxidation of the MoNbTaTiW RHEA. The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi 2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M 5 Si 3 as the inner layer. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred. After oxidation, the coating was composed of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer. The silicide layer moved toward the inside of the substrate, led to the increase of its thickness. Compared with the initial silicified layer, its structure did not change significantly. The structure and compositions of the oxide layer on the outer surface strongly depended on the oxidation temperature. Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . decision.trend: Earlier work on refractory HEAs seeking improved high-temperature oxidation resistance has largely focused on modifying bulk composition (e.g., adding ceramic reinforcements like TiC/Al2O3 or introducing elements such as Cr to form protective phases). While these approaches can enhance oxidation resistance by favoring stable oxide scales, they also alter bulk properties and can worsen mechanical performance and manufacturability. As a result, researchers still seek methods that improve surface oxidation resistance without extensive alloying additions, especially under extreme conditions.
decision.unsolved: A persistent challenge is achieving robust, stable oxide protection against high-temperature oxygen attack without resorting to major compositional changes throughout the bulk. Methods to create protective scales or diffusion barriers at the surface—while preserving underlying alloy chemistry—remain underexplored and are needed for reliable performance in oxidizing environments above 1000 °C.
decision.lever: Apply a thin, adherent, diffusion-barrier coating (e.g., via pack aluminizing or protective oxide sputter deposition) to form a stable oxide layer that resists oxygen infiltration under service temperatures above 1200 °C in air or combustion environments.
decision.why: Building on evidence that stable oxide scales (e.g., Al2O3 or Cr2O3) strongly inhibit oxidation (as shown in the literature for RHEAs with added ceramic phases or Cr-rich compositions), depositing a suitable oxide-forming layer on the existing alloy surface avoids significant bulk composition modifications. This aligns with prior findings on the protective role of oxide scales while addressing the unsolved need for simpler, surface-focused modifications to enhance oxidation resistance in refractory high-entropy alloys.
